notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Acids, bases and salts are important classes of chemical substances.
  • Acids generally produce hydrogen ions in aqueous solution.
  • Bases generally produce hydroxide ions in aqueous solution or accept protons depending on the definition used.
  • Acids and bases can neutralise each other.
  • Neutralisation commonly produces salt and water.
  • pH is used to express the acidity or basicity of aqueous solutions.
  • Indicators change colour depending on acidic or basic conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Acid + Base → Salt + Water

2. Acid
  • The word acid is derived from the Latin word acidus, meaning sour.
  • Acids generally have a sour taste.
  • Acids turn blue litmus red.
  • Acids react with many metals to release hydrogen gas.
  • Acids react with carbonates and bicarbonates to release carbon dioxide.
  • Strong acids can be corrosive.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Acid → Blue Litmus to Red

3. Base
  • Bases can neutralise acids.
  • Many bases have a bitter taste and slippery feel, but chemicals should never be tasted for identification.
  • Bases turn red litmus blue.
  • Water-soluble bases are called alkalis.
  • Strong bases can be highly corrosive.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Base → Red Litmus to Blue

4. Alkali
  • An alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
  • Sodium hydroxide is an alkali.
  • Potassium hydroxide is an alkali.
  • Calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble but its dissolved portion is alkaline.
  • All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are sufficiently soluble to be called alkalis.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

All alkalis are bases.

Not all bases are alkalis.

5. Salt
  • A salt is an ionic compound formed when acidic hydrogen ions are replaced by metal or ammonium ions.
  • Salts can be formed by neutralisation.
  • Sodium chloride is a common salt.
  • Salts may produce neutral, acidic or basic solutions depending on the ions present.
6. Arrhenius Acid
  • According to Arrhenius, an acid increases H⁺ concentration in aqueous solution.
  • Hydrochloric acid produces H⁺ and Cl⁻ in water.
  • Sulfuric acid produces hydrogen ions in water.
  • The Arrhenius definition applies mainly to aqueous solutions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Arrhenius Acid → H⁺ in Water

7. Arrhenius Base
  • According to Arrhenius, a base increases OH⁻ concentration in aqueous solution.
  • NaOH dissociates into Na⁺ and OH⁻.
  • KOH gives K⁺ and OH⁻.
  • Arrhenius base concept is mainly applied to aqueous systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Arrhenius Base → OH⁻ in Water

8. Brønsted–Lowry Acid
  • A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor.
  • A proton in acid-base chemistry corresponds to H⁺.
  • HCl donates a proton to water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Brønsted Acid → Proton Donor

9. Brønsted–Lowry Base
  • A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor.
  • Ammonia accepts a proton to form ammonium ion.
  • NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Brønsted Base → Proton Acceptor

10. Lewis Acid
  • A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair.
  • The Lewis concept is broader than the Arrhenius and Brønsted definitions.
  • H⁺ can act as a Lewis acid.
  • BF₃ is a classic Lewis acid.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lewis Acid → Electron-Pair Acceptor

11. Lewis Base
  • A Lewis base donates an electron pair.
  • NH₃ is a Lewis base.
  • OH⁻ is a Lewis base.
  • Lewis acid-base reactions involve electron-pair donation and acceptance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lewis Base → Electron-Pair Donor

12. Hydrogen Ion in Water
  • A free bare H⁺ ion does not remain isolated in water.
  • It associates with water molecules.
  • H₃O⁺ is called the hydronium ion.
  • Acidic solutions are therefore often represented using H₃O⁺.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

H⁺ + H₂O → H₃O⁺

13. Hydronium Ion
  • Formula → H₃O⁺.
  • It forms when a proton attaches to a water molecule.
  • Higher hydronium concentration generally means greater acidity.
14. Strong Acid
  • A strong acid ionises almost completely in dilute aqueous solution.
  • Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid.
  • Nitric acid is a strong acid.
  • Sulfuric acid is strong in its first ionisation.
  • Strength is different from concentration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Strong Acid → High Degree of Ionisation

15. Weak Acid
  • A weak acid ionises only partially in water.
  • Acetic acid is a weak acid.
  • Carbonic acid is weak.
  • Citric acid is weak.
  • Weak does not mean harmless or dilute.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Strength ≠ Concentration.

16. Strong Base
  • Strong bases dissociate extensively in aqueous solution.
  • Sodium hydroxide is a strong base.
  • Potassium hydroxide is a strong base.
  • Barium hydroxide is a strong base in dissolved form.
17. Weak Base
  • Weak bases ionise or react with water only partially.
  • Ammonia is a common weak base.
  • NH₃ reacts with water to produce NH₄⁺ and OH⁻.
  • Magnesium hydroxide is sparingly soluble and behaves as a weakly available base in water.
18. Concentrated vs Dilute
  • Concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute per unit solution.
  • Dilute solution contains a smaller amount.
  • A dilute strong acid may have a higher pH than a concentrated weak acid depending on concentrations.
  • Concentration and strength describe different properties.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Strong acid can be dilute.

Weak acid can be concentrated.

19. Common Strong Acids

Important strong acids include:

  • Hydrochloric acid → HCl.
  • Nitric acid → HNO₃.
  • Sulfuric acid → H₂SO₄.
  • Perchloric acid is also strong, though less common in basic school chemistry.
20. Common Weak Acids
  • Acetic acid → CH₃COOH.
  • Carbonic acid → H₂CO₃.
  • Citric acid.
  • Formic acid → HCOOH.
  • Oxalic acid → H₂C₂O₄.
  • Phosphoric acid → H₃PO₄ is weak compared with strong mineral acids.
21. Mineral Acids
  • Mineral acids are inorganic acids.
  • Hydrochloric acid.
  • Sulfuric acid.
  • Nitric acid.
  • These are widely used in laboratories and industry.
22. Organic Acids
  • Many organic acids contain the carboxyl group –COOH.
  • Acetic acid.
  • Formic acid.
  • Citric acid.
  • Lactic acid.
  • Oxalic acid.
  • Tartaric acid.
23. Hydrochloric Acid
  • Formula → HCl.
  • Hydrogen chloride is a gas in pure form.
  • Its aqueous solution is hydrochloric acid.
  • HCl is a strong acid.
  • Hydrochloric acid is present in gastric juice.
  • It helps create the acidic environment needed for digestion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gastric Acid → HCl

24. Sulfuric Acid
  • Formula → H₂SO₄.
  • It is a strong mineral acid.
  • Concentrated sulfuric acid is a powerful dehydrating agent.
  • It is widely used in fertiliser manufacture.
  • It is used in lead-acid batteries in dilute form.
  • Sulfuric acid is often called an important indicator of industrial activity because of its extensive industrial use.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lead-Acid Battery Electrolyte → H₂SO₄

25. Nitric Acid
  • Formula → HNO₃.
  • It is a strong acid.
  • It is also a strong oxidising agent.
  • It is used in fertiliser and explosives manufacture.
  • Nitric acid reacts with many metals without simply releasing hydrogen because of its oxidising nature.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Nitric acid + metal does not generally follow the simple “acid + metal → H₂” rule.

26. Acetic Acid
  • Formula → CH₃COOH.
  • It is a weak acid.
  • Vinegar contains dilute acetic acid.
  • Acetic acid gives vinegar its sour taste and smell.
  • Pure anhydrous acetic acid is called glacial acetic acid.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vinegar → Acetic Acid

27. Formic Acid
  • Formula → HCOOH.
  • It is the simplest carboxylic acid.
  • It occurs naturally in some ant secretions.
  • The name comes from Latin formica, meaning ant.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ant Sting/Secretion → Formic Acid

28. Citric Acid
  • Citric acid occurs naturally in citrus fruits.
  • Lemon and orange contain citric acid.
  • It is a weak organic acid.
  • It is used as an acidulant and preservative in foods.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Citrus Fruits → Citric Acid

29. Tartaric Acid
  • Tartaric acid occurs in tamarind, grapes and some other fruits.
  • It is used in baking powder along with sodium bicarbonate.
  • It helps neutralise the bitter taste that would otherwise remain from sodium carbonate formation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tamarind/Grapes → Tartaric Acid

30. Lactic Acid
  • Lactic acid can form during anaerobic metabolism.
  • It occurs in fermented milk products.
  • Lactic-acid bacteria convert lactose to lactic acid.
  • Yogurt/curd acidity is associated mainly with lactic acid.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Curd → Lactic Acid

31. Oxalic Acid
  • Oxalic acid occurs naturally in some plants.
  • Spinach contains oxalates.
  • It is a dicarboxylic acid.
  • Excess oxalate can contribute to formation of certain kidney stones in susceptible individuals.
32. Carbonic Acid
  • Formula → H₂CO₃.
  • It forms when carbon dioxide dissolves in water.
  • CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃.
  • Carbonic acid is weak.
  • It plays a role in natural waters and blood buffering.
33. Common Strong Bases
  • Sodium hydroxide → NaOH.
  • Potassium hydroxide → KOH.
  • Barium hydroxide → Ba(OH)₂.
  • Strong bases dissociate extensively in water.
34. Sodium Hydroxide
  • Formula → NaOH.
  • Common name → Caustic soda.
  • It is a strong alkali.
  • It is used in soap, paper and chemical manufacture.
  • It is highly corrosive.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Caustic Soda → NaOH

35. Potassium Hydroxide
  • Formula → KOH.
  • Common name → Caustic potash.
  • It is a strong alkali.
  • It is used in soft soaps and some alkaline batteries.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Caustic Potash → KOH

36. Calcium Hydroxide
  • Formula → Ca(OH)₂.
  • Common name → Slaked lime.
  • A saturated clear solution is called limewater.
  • It is used in whitewashing and neutralising acidic soils.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Slaked Lime → Ca(OH)₂

37. Magnesium Hydroxide
  • Formula → Mg(OH)₂.
  • It is only sparingly soluble in water.
  • Suspension of Mg(OH)₂ is called milk of magnesia.
  • It is used as an antacid.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Milk of Magnesia → Mg(OH)₂

38. Ammonia
  • Formula → NH₃.
  • Ammonia is a weak base.
  • It reacts with water to form NH₄⁺ and OH⁻.
  • It is highly soluble in water.
  • Aqueous ammonia is alkaline.
📌 Reaction

NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻

39. Indicators

Indicators are substances that show different colours in acidic and basic media.

Common indicators include:

  • Litmus.
  • Phenolphthalein.
  • Methyl orange.
  • Universal indicator.
  • Turmeric.
  • China rose indicator.
40. Litmus
  • Litmus is a natural indicator derived from lichens.
  • Acid turns blue litmus red.
  • Base turns red litmus blue.
  • Neutral solution causes no characteristic red/blue conversion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Acid → Blue to Red

Base → Red to Blue

41. Phenolphthalein
  • Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution.
  • It is also colourless around neutral pH.
  • It turns pink in sufficiently basic solution.
  • It is commonly used in acid-base titration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Phenolphthalein → Base = Pink

42. Methyl Orange
  • Methyl orange is red in acidic medium.
  • It is yellow in basic medium.
  • It changes through orange in its transition range.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Methyl Orange:

Acid → Red

Base → Yellow

43. Universal Indicator
  • Universal indicator is a mixture of indicators.
  • It shows different colours across a broad pH range.
  • It provides an approximate pH estimate.
  • Strong acidic solutions appear toward red.
  • Neutral solutions are generally green.
  • Basic solutions range toward blue and purple.
44. Turmeric Indicator
  • Turmeric is a natural indicator.
  • It remains yellow in acidic and neutral conditions.
  • It turns reddish-brown in basic conditions.
  • Turmeric stains may change colour when soap solution is applied.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Turmeric + Base → Reddish-Brown

45. China Rose Indicator
  • China rose or hibiscus extract is a natural acid-base indicator.
  • Acidic solutions generally produce a pink/red colour.
  • Basic solutions may produce greenish colour.
  • Exact shades depend on preparation and concentration.
46. Olfactory Indicators
  • Olfactory indicators change smell perception in acidic or basic conditions.
  • Onion, vanilla and clove are sometimes used in school demonstrations.
  • They are less quantitative than pH indicators.
47. pH
  • pH expresses acidity of an aqueous solution.
  • pH is related logarithmically to hydrogen-ion activity.
  • In dilute school-level solutions, pH ≈ −log₁₀[H⁺].
  • Lower pH means greater acidity.
  • Higher pH means greater basicity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

pH = −log[H⁺]

48. pH Scale

At approximately 25°C:

  • pH < 7 → Acidic.
  • pH = 7 → Neutral.
  • pH > 7 → Basic.
  • Common school pH scale is shown from 0 to 14.
  • More extreme pH values are possible in concentrated solutions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

The 0–14 scale is a common aqueous approximation, not an absolute universal limit.

49. Neutral pH
  • Pure water has pH approximately 7 at 25°C.
  • Neutrality means [H⁺] = [OH⁻].
  • Neutral pH changes slightly with temperature because water's ionisation changes.
50. pOH
  • pOH measures hydroxide-ion concentration.
  • pOH ≈ −log₁₀[OH⁻].
  • At 25°C in dilute aqueous solutions:
  • pH + pOH = 14.
📌 Must-Memorise

pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C

51. Ionic Product of Water
  • Water undergoes slight self-ionisation.
  • Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻].
  • At 25°C, Kw ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
  • In neutral water, [H⁺] = [OH⁻] ≈ 10⁻⁷ mol/L.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Neutral Water → [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M at 25°C

52. pH and Tenfold Change
  • The pH scale is logarithmic.
  • A decrease of one pH unit corresponds approximately to a tenfold increase in hydrogen-ion concentration.
  • pH 3 has about 10 times greater [H⁺] than pH 4.
  • pH 2 has about 100 times greater [H⁺] than pH 4.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

pH scale is logarithmic, not linear.

53. Typical pH Values — Approximate
  • Gastric juice → about 1–3.
  • Lemon juice → about 2.
  • Vinegar → about 2–3.
  • Pure water → about 7.
  • Human blood → about 7.35–7.45.
  • Baking-soda solution → mildly basic.
  • Soap solution → basic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Human Blood → Slightly Basic, pH ~7.4

54. Acid in Stomach
  • Gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid.
  • HCl activates pepsin from its precursor and provides acidic conditions for protein digestion.
  • Excess gastric acidity can cause discomfort.
  • Antacids neutralise excess acid.
55. Antacid
  • Antacids are basic substances used to neutralise excess stomach acid.
  • Magnesium hydroxide is used.
  • Aluminium hydroxide may be used.
  • Calcium carbonate is also used in some antacids.
  • Sodium bicarbonate can neutralise acid but is not always preferred for regular antacid use.
56. Tooth Decay and pH
  • Oral bacteria metabolise sugars and produce acids.
  • Tooth enamel begins to dissolve more rapidly below a critical pH, often cited around 5.5.
  • Brushing removes plaque and reduces acid exposure.
  • Fluoride can increase enamel resistance to acid attack.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tooth Decay Risk ↑ below pH ~5.5

57. Soil pH
  • Soil pH affects nutrient availability and plant growth.
  • Different crops prefer different pH ranges.
  • Acidic soil can be treated with lime.
  • Calcium oxide, calcium hydroxide or limestone may be used depending on agricultural practice.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Acidic Soil → Lime Treatment

58. Acid Rain
  • Acid rain has lower pH than normal rain.
  • Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form acids in the atmosphere.
  • Sulfuric and nitric acids are important contributors.
  • Acid rain damages lakes, soils, vegetation, buildings and monuments.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Acid Rain → SO₂ + NOₓ

59. Normal Rainwater
  • Normal rainwater is slightly acidic because atmospheric CO₂ dissolves in it.
  • Carbonic acid forms.
  • Natural rain pH is often around 5.6 in clean air.
  • Acid rain is conventionally defined as precipitation significantly more acidic than this natural baseline.
60. Neutralisation
  • Neutralisation is a reaction between acid and base.
  • Salt and water are commonly produced.
  • H⁺ combines with OH⁻ to form water.
  • Neutralisation is generally exothermic.
📌 Ionic Equation

H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O

61. Hydrochloric Acid + Sodium Hydroxide

Reaction:

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

  • Hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide.
  • Sodium chloride and water form.
62. Sulfuric Acid + Sodium Hydroxide

Reaction:

H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

  • Two moles of NaOH are required for complete neutralisation of one mole of H₂SO₄ in this ideal stoichiometric reaction.
63. Acid + Metal

General reaction:

Acid + Reactive Metal → Salt + Hydrogen

Example:

Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂

  • Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series commonly release hydrogen from dilute non-oxidising acids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Acid + Metal → H₂ Gas

64. Test for Hydrogen Gas
  • Hydrogen gas burns with a characteristic “pop” sound when a flame is brought near a small sample.
  • This is the traditional laboratory test for hydrogen.
  • Appropriate safety precautions are essential.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hydrogen Test → Pop Sound

65. Acid + Metal Carbonate

General reaction:

Acid + Carbonate → Salt + Water + Carbon Dioxide

Example:

2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Acid + Carbonate → CO₂

66. Acid + Metal Bicarbonate

General reaction:

Acid + Bicarbonate → Salt + Water + CO₂

Example:

HCl + NaHCO₃ → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂

67. Test for Carbon Dioxide
  • CO₂ is passed through limewater.
  • Limewater turns milky due to formation of calcium carbonate.
  • Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

CO₂ Test → Limewater Turns Milky

68. Excess Carbon Dioxide in Limewater
  • Passing excess CO₂ through milky limewater can clear the solution.
  • Soluble calcium bicarbonate forms.

Reaction:

CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂

69. Base + Non-Metal Oxide
  • Many non-metal oxides are acidic.
  • They react with bases to form salt and water.
  • Example:
  • 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O.
70. Acid + Metal Oxide
  • Many metal oxides are basic.
  • Acid + Basic metal oxide → Salt + Water.
  • Example:
  • CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O.
71. Amphoteric Oxides
  • Amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases.
  • Aluminium oxide is amphoteric.
  • Zinc oxide is amphoteric.
  • Al₂O₃ and ZnO are common TNPSC examples.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Amphoteric → Reacts with Acid and Base

72. Acidic Oxides
  • Many non-metal oxides are acidic.
  • CO₂ is acidic.
  • SO₂ is acidic.
  • SO₃ is acidic.
  • They can react with bases.
73. Basic Oxides
  • Many metal oxides are basic.
  • Na₂O is basic.
  • CaO is basic.
  • MgO is basic.
  • They react with acids to form salts and water.
74. Neutral Oxides

Common neutral oxides include:

  • Carbon monoxide → CO.
  • Nitric oxide → NO.
  • Nitrous oxide → N₂O in basic classification.
  • They show neither strongly acidic nor basic behaviour with water.
75. Salt Formation — Acid + Base

Example:

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

This is neutralisation.

76. Salt Formation — Acid + Metal

Example:

2HCl + Mg → MgCl₂ + H₂

77. Salt Formation — Acid + Carbonate

Example:

2HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂

78. Salt Formation — Acid + Metal Oxide

Example:

H₂SO₄ + CuO → CuSO₄ + H₂O

79. Normal Salt
  • A normal salt forms when all replaceable acidic hydrogen ions are replaced.
  • NaCl is a normal salt.
  • Na₂SO₄ is a normal salt.
  • KNO₃ is a normal salt.
80. Acid Salt
  • Acid salts retain replaceable hydrogen from a polyprotic acid.
  • Sodium hydrogen carbonate → NaHCO₃.
  • Sodium hydrogen sulfate → NaHSO₄.
  • Acid salts do not necessarily produce acidic solutions in all cases.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

“Acid salt” refers to composition, not automatically to solution pH.

81. Basic Salt
  • Basic salts contain hydroxyl groups or arise from partial neutralisation of polyhydroxy bases in traditional classification.
  • Some basic salts can form when a base is incompletely neutralised by acid.
  • Their exact chemistry varies with the compound.
82. Double Salt
  • Double salts crystallise together in a definite ratio but dissociate into their component ions in water.
  • Potash alum is a common example.
  • Mohr's salt is another example.
83. Complex Salt
  • Complex salts contain complex ions.
  • Potassium ferrocyanide is a classic example.
  • Complex ions retain their identity in solution.
84. Sodium Chloride
  • Formula → NaCl.
  • Common name → Common salt.
  • It is obtained from seawater and rock salt.
  • It is an important raw material in the chlor-alkali industry.
  • It is essential in diet in appropriate amounts.
85. Chlor-Alkali Process
  • Electrolysis of brine produces sodium hydroxide, chlorine and hydrogen.
  • Brine is concentrated aqueous sodium chloride.
  • Chlorine forms at the anode.
  • Hydrogen forms at the cathode.
  • Sodium hydroxide remains in solution.
📌 Overall Reaction

2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Brine Electrolysis → NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂

86. Sodium Hydroxide from Brine
  • Sodium hydroxide is produced industrially by chlor-alkali electrolysis.
  • It is used in soap, paper and textile industries.
87. Chlorine from Brine
  • Chlorine gas is produced at the anode during brine electrolysis.
  • Chlorine is used in water disinfection and manufacture of many chemicals.
  • Chlorine is toxic at high concentrations.
88. Hydrogen from Brine
  • Hydrogen gas is produced at the cathode.
  • It can be used in chemical manufacture and energy applications.
89. Baking Soda
  • Chemical name → Sodium hydrogen carbonate / Sodium bicarbonate.
  • Formula → NaHCO₃.
  • It is mildly basic.
  • It is used in baking powder.
  • It is used in some fire extinguishers.
  • It can neutralise acids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Baking Soda → NaHCO₃

90. Heating Baking Soda

Reaction:

2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O

  • Carbon dioxide released helps dough or batter rise.
  • Sodium carbonate remains.
91. Baking Powder
  • Baking powder contains sodium bicarbonate and an edible weak acid, commonly tartaric acid or similar acid salts.
  • On wetting and heating, carbon dioxide is produced.
  • CO₂ makes cakes and bread porous and soft.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Baking Powder → Baking Soda + Edible Acid

92. Washing Soda
  • Chemical name → Sodium carbonate decahydrate.
  • Formula → Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
  • It is used in cleaning.
  • It is used to soften hard water.
  • It is used in glass, soap and paper industries.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Washing Soda → Na₂CO₃·10H₂O

93. Sodium Carbonate
  • Formula → Na₂CO₃.
  • It is basic.
  • It can be produced from sodium bicarbonate by heating.
  • Hydrated sodium carbonate forms washing soda.
94. Water of Crystallisation
  • Water of crystallisation is a fixed number of water molecules chemically associated within a crystalline salt.
  • CuSO₄·5H₂O contains five water molecules per formula unit.
  • Na₂CO₃·10H₂O contains ten.
  • Water of crystallisation affects crystal properties and colour.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water of Crystallisation → Fixed Water in Crystal

95. Copper Sulfate Pentahydrate
  • Formula → CuSO₄·5H₂O.
  • Common name → Blue vitriol.
  • Hydrated copper sulfate is blue.
  • On strong heating, it loses water and becomes nearly white anhydrous CuSO₄.
  • Adding water restores the blue colour.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Blue Vitriol → CuSO₄·5H₂O

96. Ferrous Sulfate Heptahydrate
  • Formula → FeSO₄·7H₂O.
  • Common name → Green vitriol.
  • It forms pale green crystals.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Green Vitriol → FeSO₄·7H₂O

97. Epsom Salt
  • Chemical name → Magnesium sulfate heptahydrate.
  • Formula → MgSO₄·7H₂O.
  • It is known as Epsom salt.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Epsom Salt → MgSO₄·7H₂O

98. Glauber's Salt
  • Chemical name → Sodium sulfate decahydrate.
  • Formula → Na₂SO₄·10H₂O.
  • It is called Glauber's salt.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Glauber's Salt → Na₂SO₄·10H₂O

99. Plaster of Paris
  • Chemical name → Calcium sulfate hemihydrate.
  • Formula → CaSO₄·½H₂O.
  • It is commonly called POP.
  • It is produced by heating gypsum carefully.
  • It sets into hard gypsum when mixed with water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Plaster of Paris → CaSO₄·½H₂O

100. Gypsum
  • Formula → CaSO₄·2H₂O.
  • Gypsum is calcium sulfate dihydrate.
  • Heating gypsum produces plaster of Paris under controlled conditions.
📌 Reaction

CaSO₄·2H₂O → CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O

101. Setting of Plaster of Paris
  • POP reacts with water.
  • It forms gypsum.
  • The process produces a hard solid mass.
  • It is used in casts, moulds and decorative work.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

POP + Water → Gypsum

102. Bleaching Powder
  • Bleaching powder is commonly represented in school chemistry as CaOCl₂.
  • It is manufactured by passing chlorine over dry slaked lime.
  • It is used for bleaching and disinfection.
  • It releases available chlorine under suitable conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bleaching Powder → CaOCl₂

103. Preparation of Bleaching Powder

Simplified reaction:

Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O

  • Slaked lime reacts with chlorine.
104. Uses of Bleaching Powder
  • Bleaching cotton and linen.
  • Bleaching wood pulp.
  • Disinfecting drinking-water systems under controlled dosing.
  • Oxidising agent in chemical processes.
105. Common Salt as Raw Material

NaCl is used to manufacture:

  • NaOH.
  • Chlorine.
  • Hydrogen.
  • Baking soda.
  • Washing soda.
  • Hydrochloric acid in industrial chemical processes.
106. pH of Salt Solutions
  • Salts from strong acid + strong base are often approximately neutral.
  • Salts from strong acid + weak base often give acidic solutions.
  • Salts from weak acid + strong base often give basic solutions.
  • Hydrolysis of ions determines solution pH.
107. Neutral Salt Example
  • NaCl is formed from strong acid HCl and strong base NaOH.
  • Aqueous NaCl solution is approximately neutral under ideal dilute conditions.
108. Acidic Salt Solution Example
  • Ammonium chloride → NH₄Cl.
  • It is formed from strong acid HCl and weak base NH₃.
  • Its aqueous solution is acidic because NH₄⁺ hydrolyses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NH₄Cl Solution → Acidic

109. Basic Salt Solution Example
  • Sodium carbonate → Na₂CO₃.
  • It is derived from weak carbonic acid and strong sodium hydroxide.
  • Its aqueous solution is basic because carbonate ion hydrolyses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Na₂CO₃ Solution → Basic

110. Salt Hydrolysis
  • Hydrolysis is reaction of salt ions with water.
  • It may produce H₃O⁺ or OH⁻.
  • This can make a salt solution acidic or basic.
  • Not every salt solution is neutral.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Salt ≠ Always neutral.

111. Buffer Solution
  • A buffer resists large changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
  • Acidic buffers commonly contain a weak acid and its conjugate base.
  • Basic buffers commonly contain a weak base and its conjugate acid.
  • Buffers are important in biological systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Buffer → Resists pH Change

112. Blood Buffer
  • Human blood maintains pH in a narrow range around 7.4.
  • Bicarbonate/carbonic-acid buffering is important.
  • Protein and phosphate buffers also contribute.
  • Large pH deviations are physiologically dangerous.
113. pH in Human Body
  • Stomach → Strongly acidic.
  • Blood → Slightly basic.
  • Small intestine → Generally mildly alkaline.
  • Different enzymes work best at different pH values.
114. Acid-Base Titration
  • Titration is used to determine concentration of an acid or base.
  • A solution of known concentration is gradually added to another solution.
  • Indicator or pH meter identifies the endpoint.
  • A burette delivers measured volumes accurately.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Titration → Concentration Determination

115. Burette
  • A burette accurately delivers variable volumes of solution.
  • It is commonly used in titration.
  • Volume is read from graduations.
116. Pipette
  • A pipette transfers a precise fixed or measured volume.
  • Volumetric pipettes are used in quantitative analysis.
117. Conical Flask
  • Conical flask commonly contains the solution being titrated.
  • Its shape allows swirling with low risk of spilling.
  • It is also called an Erlenmeyer flask.
118. Endpoint
  • Endpoint is the observed point at which an indicator changes colour.
  • Equivalence point is the theoretical point at which stoichiometric quantities have reacted.
  • A good indicator makes the endpoint close to the equivalence point.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Endpoint and equivalence point are related but not exactly identical concepts.

119. Acid-Base Indicator Choice
  • Strong acid–strong base titrations can use several indicators.
  • Weak acid–strong base titrations commonly use phenolphthalein.
  • Strong acid–weak base titrations commonly use methyl orange.
  • Indicator should change colour near the equivalence-point pH.
120. pH Meter
  • A pH meter measures pH electrically.
  • It commonly uses a glass electrode and reference electrode.
  • It provides more precise pH measurement than colour indicators.
121. Acidic Nature of Non-Metal Oxides
  • CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃.
  • SO₂ dissolves in water forming acidic species.
  • SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.
  • Non-metal oxides are often acidic.
122. Basic Nature of Metal Oxides
  • Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH.
  • CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂.
  • Many metal oxides produce basic solutions or neutralise acids.
123. Quicklime
  • Formula → CaO.
  • Common name → Quicklime.
  • It is a basic oxide.
  • It reacts vigorously with water to form slaked lime.
  • The reaction is exothermic.
📌 Reaction

CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + Heat

124. Slaked Lime
  • Formula → Ca(OH)₂.
  • It is used in whitewashing.
  • It neutralises acidic soil.
  • Limewater is its clear saturated solution.
125. Whitewashing
  • Slaked lime is applied to walls.
  • It slowly reacts with CO₂ in air.
  • Calcium carbonate forms.
  • This produces a hard white finish.
📌 Reaction

Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O

126. Hard Water and Washing Soda
  • Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions.
  • Washing soda can precipitate these ions as insoluble carbonates.
  • This reduces hardness.
  • Sodium carbonate is therefore used as a water-softening agent.
127. Temporary Hardness
  • Temporary hardness is mainly due to bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium.
  • Boiling can remove temporary hardness.
  • Insoluble carbonates may precipitate.
128. Permanent Hardness
  • Permanent hardness is mainly due to soluble sulfates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium.
  • Boiling does not remove permanent hardness effectively.
  • Washing soda or ion-exchange processes can remove it.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Temporary Hardness → Removed by Boiling

Permanent Hardness → Not by Boiling

129. Acidic Soil
  • Excessively acidic soil may reduce crop productivity.
  • Lime materials can neutralise acidity.
  • Quicklime, slaked lime or limestone may be used depending on agricultural conditions.
130. Basic Soil
  • Excessively alkaline soil may also reduce nutrient availability.
  • Organic matter and appropriate soil amendments may help depending on cause.
  • Soil treatment should be based on soil testing.
131. Acid-Base Reaction in Ant Sting
  • Ant stings are commonly associated with formic acid.
  • Mild basic materials such as sodium bicarbonate have traditionally been cited for neutralisation in school chemistry.
  • Real sting management should prioritise washing and appropriate first aid rather than relying on household neutralisation.
132. Bee and Wasp Sting Trap
  • Stings contain complex mixtures of biologically active substances.
  • The simplistic “bee sting acid, wasp sting alkali” rule is not chemically reliable for real medical treatment.
  • TNPSC questions may still use simplified textbook acid-base examples, but actual first aid should not depend on neutralisation assumptions.
133. Soap
  • Soap solutions are generally alkaline.
  • Soap contains sodium or potassium salts of fatty acids.
  • Soap can turn red litmus blue.
  • Strongly alkaline soap can irritate sensitive skin.
134. Shampoo
  • Shampoos are formulated near mildly acidic to neutral pH depending on product.
  • Hair and skin products are designed to avoid strongly acidic or alkaline conditions.
  • pH influences hair cuticle and skin compatibility.
135. Toothpaste
  • Toothpaste often contains mildly basic components.
  • It helps neutralise acids produced by oral bacteria.
  • It also contains abrasives and fluoride in many formulations.
136. Acidic Food Examples
  • Lemon → Citric acid.
  • Vinegar → Acetic acid.
  • Tamarind → Tartaric and other organic acids.
  • Curd → Lactic acid.
  • Tomato → Citric and malic acids.
  • Apple → Malic acid is an important acid.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lemon → Citric

Vinegar → Acetic

Curd → Lactic

Ant → Formic

137. Acids and Metals — Reactivity
  • Highly reactive metals react readily with dilute acids.
  • Zinc reacts with dilute HCl.
  • Magnesium reacts with dilute HCl.
  • Copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute HCl because it lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series.
  • Oxidising acids can react differently.
138. Acid Safety
  • Concentrated acids can cause severe burns.
  • Acid should generally be added slowly to water during dilution.
  • Adding water directly to concentrated acid can cause violent boiling and splashing.
  • Protective equipment is required in laboratories.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dilution Rule → Add Acid to Water

139. Why Add Acid to Water
  • Diluting concentrated acid releases heat.
  • Water present in larger quantity absorbs the heat more safely.
  • Adding a small amount of water to concentrated acid can cause rapid local heating and splashing.
📌 Memory

Always Acid → Water

140. Base Safety
  • Strong bases such as NaOH and KOH are highly corrosive.
  • They can cause deep chemical burns.
  • They must be handled with protective equipment.
  • Dissolving NaOH in water releases considerable heat.
141. Exothermic Neutralisation
  • Strong acid–strong base neutralisation is generally exothermic.
  • Formation of water from H⁺ and OH⁻ releases heat.
  • Temperature of the solution usually rises.
142. Common Acid Formulae
  • Hydrochloric acid → HCl.
  • Sulfuric acid → H₂SO₄.
  • Nitric acid → HNO₃.
  • Carbonic acid → H₂CO₃.
  • Acetic acid → CH₃COOH.
  • Formic acid → HCOOH.
  • Phosphoric acid → H₃PO₄.
143. Common Base Formulae
  • Sodium hydroxide → NaOH.
  • Potassium hydroxide → KOH.
  • Calcium hydroxide → Ca(OH)₂.
  • Magnesium hydroxide → Mg(OH)₂.
  • Barium hydroxide → Ba(OH)₂.
  • Ammonia → NH₃ as weak base.
144. Common Salt Formulae
  • Common salt → NaCl.
  • Baking soda → NaHCO₃.
  • Washing soda → Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
  • Blue vitriol → CuSO₄·5H₂O.
  • Green vitriol → FeSO₄·7H₂O.
  • Epsom salt → MgSO₄·7H₂O.
  • Glauber's salt → Na₂SO₄·10H₂O.
  • Gypsum → CaSO₄·2H₂O.
  • Plaster of Paris → CaSO₄·½H₂O.
145. Important Colour-Indicator Facts
  • Blue litmus + acid → Red.
  • Red litmus + base → Blue.
  • Phenolphthalein + acid → Colourless.
  • Phenolphthalein + base → Pink.
  • Methyl orange + acid → Red.
  • Methyl orange + base → Yellow.
  • Universal indicator at neutral pH → Green.
  • Turmeric + base → Reddish-brown.
146. Important pH Facts
  • pH < 7 → Acidic.
  • pH 7 → Neutral at about 25°C.
  • pH > 7 → Basic.
  • Lower pH → Greater acidity.
  • Higher pH → Greater basicity.
  • One pH unit corresponds to tenfold [H⁺] change.
  • Blood → approximately 7.4.
  • Gastric juice → strongly acidic.
  • Tooth enamel begins greater acid dissolution below about 5.5.
147. Important Reactions

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂

CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O

NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + CO₂ + H₂O

CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂

Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O

2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O

148. Important Scientist–Concept Pairs
  • Svante Arrhenius → Acid/base ion theory in water.
  • Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry → Proton donor/acceptor theory.
  • Gilbert N. Lewis → Electron-pair acid-base theory.
  • Søren Sørensen → Introduced the pH concept in 1909.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sørensen → pH → 1909

149. pH History
  • The pH concept was introduced by Danish chemist Søren P. L. Sørensen.
  • It was introduced in 1909.
  • The concept was developed while working at the Carlsberg Laboratory.
150. TNPSC Traps
  • Acid turns blue litmus red.
  • Base turns red litmus blue.
  • Alkali means water-soluble base.
  • Acid strength and acid concentration are different.
  • Weak acid can be concentrated.
  • Strong acid can be dilute.
  • HCl is strong.
  • Acetic acid is weak.
  • NH₃ is a weak base.
  • pH scale is logarithmic.
  • pH 3 is ten times more acidic in [H⁺] than pH 4.
  • Neutral pH is about 7 only under ordinary room-temperature aqueous conditions.
  • Phenolphthalein is pink in base.
  • Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base.
  • Turmeric turns reddish-brown in base.
  • Acid + carbonate releases CO₂.
  • CO₂ turns limewater milky.
  • Acid + reactive metal releases H₂ except oxidising-acid complications.
  • Nitric acid is an oxidising acid.
  • Neutralisation is generally exothermic.
  • Not every salt solution is neutral.
  • NH₄Cl solution is acidic.
  • Na₂CO₃ solution is basic.
  • NaCl solution is approximately neutral.
  • Washing soda is Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
  • Baking soda is NaHCO₃.
  • POP is CaSO₄·½H₂O.
  • Gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O.
  • Blue vitriol is CuSO₄·5H₂O.
  • Green vitriol is FeSO₄·7H₂O.
  • Epsom salt is MgSO₄·7H₂O.
  • Bleaching powder is represented as CaOCl₂ in school chemistry.
  • Brine electrolysis gives NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.
  • Acid rain is mainly linked to SO₂ and NOₓ.
  • Human blood is slightly basic.
  • Gastric juice contains HCl.
  • Acid should be added to water during dilution, not water to concentrated acid.
151. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Acid → H⁺.
  • Base → OH⁻.
  • Brønsted acid → Proton donor.
  • Brønsted base → Proton acceptor.
  • Lewis acid → Electron-pair acceptor.
  • Lewis base → Electron-pair donor.
  • Acid litmus → Blue to red.
  • Base litmus → Red to blue.
  • Phenolphthalein base → Pink.
  • Methyl orange acid → Red.
  • pH < 7 → Acid.
  • pH 7 → Neutral.
  • pH > 7 → Base.
  • HCl → Gastric acid.
  • Vinegar → Acetic.
  • Lemon → Citric.
  • Curd → Lactic.
  • Ant → Formic.
  • Caustic soda → NaOH.
  • Caustic potash → KOH.
  • Milk of magnesia → Mg(OH)₂.
  • Common salt → NaCl.
  • Baking soda → NaHCO₃.
  • Washing soda → Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
  • POP → CaSO₄·½H₂O.
  • Gypsum → CaSO₄·2H₂O.
  • Blue vitriol → CuSO₄·5H₂O.
  • Acid + carbonate → CO₂.
  • Neutralisation → Salt + water.
  • Brine electrolysis → NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What does an acid do to blue litmus? → Turns it red.
  • What does a base do to red litmus? → Turns it blue.
  • Water-soluble base called? → Alkali.
  • Arrhenius acid produces? → H⁺ in water.
  • Arrhenius base produces? → OH⁻ in water.
  • Brønsted acid? → Proton donor.
  • Brønsted base? → Proton acceptor.
  • Lewis acid? → Electron-pair acceptor.
  • Lewis base? → Electron-pair donor.
  • Hydrated form of H⁺ in water? → H₃O⁺.
  • Strong acid means? → Highly ionised in water.
  • Weak acid means? → Partially ionised.
  • Is strength same as concentration? → No.
  • Strong mineral acids commonly asked? → HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃.
  • Weak acid in vinegar? → Acetic acid.
  • Acetic-acid formula? → CH₃COOH.
  • Acid in lemon? → Citric acid.
  • Acid in curd? → Lactic acid.
  • Acid associated with ants? → Formic acid.
  • Formic-acid formula? → HCOOH.
  • Acid in gastric juice? → Hydrochloric acid.
  • Formula of sulfuric acid? → H₂SO₄.
  • Electrolyte in lead-acid battery? → Dilute sulfuric acid.
  • Formula of nitric acid? → HNO₃.
  • Strong alkali NaOH called? → Caustic soda.
  • KOH called? → Caustic potash.
  • Slaked lime? → Ca(OH)₂.
  • Milk of magnesia? → Mg(OH)₂.
  • Ammonia is strong or weak base? → Weak base.
  • Indicator derived from lichens? → Litmus.
  • Phenolphthalein colour in acid? → Colourless.
  • Phenolphthalein colour in base? → Pink.
  • Methyl-orange colour in acid? → Red.
  • Methyl-orange colour in base? → Yellow.
  • Universal indicator colour around neutral pH? → Green.
  • Turmeric colour in basic solution? → Reddish-brown.
  • pH formula? → −log[H⁺].
  • Acidic pH? → Below 7.
  • Neutral pH at about 25°C? → 7.
  • Basic pH? → Above 7.
  • pH + pOH at 25°C? → 14.
  • Kw at 25°C approximately? → 10⁻¹⁴.
  • [H⁺] in neutral water at 25°C? → 10⁻⁷ mol/L.
  • Is pH scale linear? → No, logarithmic.
  • Difference of one pH unit means what [H⁺] change? → Tenfold.
  • Approximate blood pH? → About 7.4.
  • Gastric juice pH? → Strongly acidic, roughly 1–3.
  • Critical enamel-dissolution pH often cited? → About 5.5.
  • What is neutralisation? → Acid + base reaction producing salt and usually water.
  • Net ionic neutralisation equation? → H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
  • HCl + NaOH gives? → NaCl + H₂O.
  • Acid + reactive metal gives? → Salt + hydrogen.
  • Hydrogen gas test? → Pop sound.
  • Acid + carbonate gives? → Salt + water + CO₂.
  • CO₂ test? → Turns limewater milky.
  • Why does limewater become milky? → CaCO₃ precipitate forms.
  • Acid + basic oxide gives? → Salt + water.
  • Examples of amphoteric oxides? → Al₂O₃ and ZnO.
  • Common neutral oxide? → CO.
  • Common salt formula? → NaCl.
  • Baking soda formula? → NaHCO₃.
  • Washing soda formula? → Na₂CO₃·10H₂O.
  • Blue vitriol formula? → CuSO₄·5H₂O.
  • Green vitriol formula? → FeSO₄·7H₂O.
  • Epsom salt formula? → MgSO₄·7H₂O.
  • Glauber's salt formula? → Na₂SO₄·10H₂O.
  • Gypsum formula? → CaSO₄·2H₂O.
  • Plaster of Paris formula? → CaSO₄·½H₂O.
  • Bleaching powder school formula? → CaOCl₂.
  • Quicklime? → CaO.
  • Slaked lime? → Ca(OH)₂.
  • What happens when POP is mixed with water? → It sets to gypsum.
  • What is water of crystallisation? → Fixed water molecules associated with crystalline salt.
  • Brine means? → Concentrated aqueous NaCl.
  • Products of brine electrolysis? → NaOH, Cl₂ and H₂.
  • Chlorine produced at which electrode in brine electrolysis? → Anode.
  • Hydrogen produced at? → Cathode.
  • Heating baking soda gives? → Na₂CO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O.
  • Why does baking powder make cakes rise? → CO₂ gas is released.
  • Washing soda used for? → Cleaning and softening hard water.
  • Salt from strong acid + strong base generally gives? → Approximately neutral solution.
  • NH₄Cl solution? → Acidic.
  • Na₂CO₃ solution? → Basic.
  • Why can salt solutions be acidic/basic? → Hydrolysis of ions.
  • Buffer means? → Solution resisting large pH changes.
  • Important blood buffer? → Bicarbonate/carbonic-acid system.
  • Instrument used to measure pH accurately? → pH meter.
  • Instrument used to deliver titrant? → Burette.
  • Instrument used to transfer fixed precise volume? → Pipette.
  • Titration used for? → Determining solution concentration.
  • Acid rain mainly caused by? → Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
  • Approximate natural rain pH? → Around 5.6.
  • Acidic soil can be treated with? → Lime.
  • Temporary hardness mainly due to? → Calcium and magnesium bicarbonates.
  • Temporary hardness removed by? → Boiling.
  • Permanent hardness due mainly to? → Calcium/magnesium chlorides and sulfates.
  • Permanent hardness removed by boiling? → No.
  • Water-softening salt commonly used? → Washing soda.
  • Why is pressure/heat released when diluting concentrated acid important? → Dilution is strongly exothermic.
  • Correct dilution rule? → Add acid slowly to water.
  • Who introduced pH concept? → Søren P. L. Sørensen.
  • Year of pH concept? → 1909.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Acid → H⁺; Base → OH⁻; pH <7 acid, >7 base; Baking soda → NaHCO₃; Washing soda → Na₂CO₃·10H₂O; POP → CaSO₄·½H₂O; Brine electrolysis → NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂.
